tier_reason: hiae-aead/benchmarks publishes the harness (hiae/benchmark.c, a vendored copy of the libhiae sources, and aes128-gcm-openssl/benchmark.c) and states the setup: Apple clang 21.0.0, -O3 -mcpu=native, OpenSSL 3.6.4, Apple M5 Max. Its 64 KB table shows HiAE AEAD encryption at 266.7 Gbps against 70.8 Gbps for AES-128-GCM.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On Apple M5 Max with 64 KB messages, HiAE (a vendored libhiae copy) reaches 266.7 Gbps AEAD encryption against 70.8 Gbps for OpenSSL 3.6.4 AES-128-GCM (~3.77x, derived from page data). Separately, the designers' ePrint 2025/377 paper benchmarks their own Concyclics/HiAE implementation, not libhiae, against OpenSSL 3.0. Its abstract claims over 340 Gbps (x86) and 180 Gbps (ARM) for AEAD. Table 10, AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 16384-byte messages: AEAD 340.02 Gbps vs AES-256-GCM 51.90 Gbps (~6.6x, derived from paper data); encryption-only 352.73 Gbps vs AES-256-CTR 95.71 Gbps (~3.7x, derived). The record's 269.01 vs 84.09 Gbps pair is encryption-only at 1024 bytes against AES-256-CTR, not AEAD against AES-256-GCM.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: M5 Max run: Apple clang 21.0.0 on macOS 26, -O3 -mcpu=native, OpenSSL 3.6.4. Paper: GCC 11.4 -O3 on the x86 servers (Ubuntu 22.04) and on the desktop (Windows 11 WSL2, Ubuntu 22.04, which includes the 7950X), and GCC 14 on the Apple laptops.
corrections.hardware: Apple M5 Max (macOS 26) for the AES-GCM comparison. The page also has a Zen 4 (Ryzen 7 7700, 3.8 GHz fixed) run, but its text table gives no AES-GCM figure. The paper covers 14 CPUs (Table 9), including the AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and Intel Xeon W9-3495X.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark repo (hiae-aead/benchmarks, no LICENSE file) is maintained by libhiae's main author (jedisct1), so these are first-party measurements of a vendored libhiae copy. The ePrint 2025/377 figures measure a different implementation, the designers' Concyclics/HiAE (no license). The paper is still an ePrint preprint (4 revisions, last 2025-06-04) and no Crossref record for it was found. It accompanies draft-pham-cfrg-hiae (rev 06), which is an individual draft and not yet an RFC.

notes: libhiae and the catalogued concyclics/hiae are separate code bases. libhiae is jedisct1/Frank Denis's full implementation (117 of about 120 commits are his; the HiAE designer Concyclics made 2); it is not a fork, port or binding. Denis (Fastly) co-authors the IETF HiAE draft with the Huawei designers. The benchmark-page numbers are Denis's own runs of libhiae code; the paper numbers are the designers' runs of their own repo, so the two entries cover the same algorithm and one may be redundant.

tier_reason: The hiae-aead/benchmarks ROCCA-S row measures rocca-s/rocca-s.c, the KDDI Corporation reference C code (MIT, (c) 2023 KDDI), not this Rust crate. The crate's README currently has no numbers: its old table (EPYC 7543, rocca-s 5.09 G/s vs RustCrypto aes128-gcm 1.24 G/s) was deleted by the author in commit f4c5181 (2024-10-21), with the message that a Rust _mm_aesenc_si128 bug 'makes performance not great'.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No current numbers for this crate. The README benchmarks were withdrawn in Oct 2024. The hiae-aead/benchmarks ROCCA-S figures (208.1 Gbps M5 Max, 174.6 Gbps Zen 4, AEAD encryption at 64 KB) belong to the vendored KDDI C reference implementation, not to rust-rocca-s.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 8 stars; crates.io crate 'rocca' v0.3.2, about 7.7k all-time downloads
corrections.caveats: The license is declared only in Cargo.toml and on crates.io (MIT); the repo has no LICENSE text file. The crate's benches/benchmark.rs compares against RustCrypto aes-gcm and BoringSSL AES-128-GCM (16 KB) but publishes no results. The author noted degraded x86 performance from a Rust _mm_aesenc_si128 bug.

notes: rust-rocca-s is Frank Denis's (jedisct1) pure-Rust port of his own zig-rocca-s; its README says 'ported from the Zig implementation', and it is not bindings (src has lib.rs, aes_ni.rs, softaes.rs). It is independent of the KDDI C code. The shootout numbers are not its own measurements. The same shootout ROCCA-S row is also not zig-rocca-s code, which matters for the separate zig-rocca-s verification. The algorithm is already covered by the zig-rocca-s entry.

tier_reason: Upgraded from D. NEWS.md (v1.12, released 2022-06-12) gives first-party CRC-32 figures on Apple M1: about 67 GB/s for libdeflate vs 31 GB/s for the Apple-provided zlib. It gives no compiler, flags or input details, although the checksum tool (programs/checksum.c, -Z selects zlib) and scripts/checksum_benchmarks.sh are public.

corrections.claimed_speedup: NEWS.md v1.12: CRC-32 on large inputs on Apple M1 'is now about 67 GB/s, compared to 8 GB/s before, or 31 GB/s with the Apple-provided zlib' (~2.2x vs zlib crc32, derived from page data). Separately, the README says libdeflate 'is significantly faster than the zlib library' (general claim).
corrections.hardware: Apple M1 (for the v1.12 CRC-32 figure)
corrections.caveats: The only numeric CRC-32 vs zlib figure is a one-line first-party note in NEWS.md for v1.12 (2022). It was measured on Apple M1 against Apple's system zlib (not necessarily stock zlib) and gives no compiler, flags or input description. The CRC code has changed since then (v1.20 added VPCLMULQDQ; later releases tuned Neoverse V). No x86 or current results table against zlib is published, though the benchmark tooling (programs/checksum.c, scripts/checksum_benchmarks.sh) is public. The usage list (libtiff, htslib, OpenEXR, uWebSockets) was not re-verified.
